name: Lusaamia
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Marlo, Michael R. & Aaron P. Brown. 2003 [2002]. Segmental duration in Lusaamia: a phonetic study. IULC Working Papers Online 2 (version date 1/28/2003), 25 pp. Bloomington: Indiana University Linguistics Club. (the Internet Archive copy of the formerly public IULC WP Online PDF.) Companion: Marlo, Michael R. 2002. Reduplication in Lusaamia. IULC Working Papers Online 2 (version date 10/20/2002), 32 pp.
catalog_locator: Marlo & Brown 2003 p. 16, sec. 5.5.1 'Target vowels' under 5.5 'Effect of position: reduplicant vs. base', discussion of Table 13; also p. 1 abstract, p. 4 (sec. 2 end and 3 'Hypotheses'), p. 18 (two hypotheses), p. 21 (conclusion). Marlo 2002 p. 26-27 and fn. 24.
catalog_quote: The data in Table 13 show that, except for the short vowels, V1—the vowel of the reduplicant—is significantly shorter than V3—the vowel of the base—as demonstrated by a paired sample t-test (t(19)= -3.154, p < .05). This could be an effect of penultimate stress in Lusaamia, such that vowels in penultimate position—the stressed position—are significantly longer than the vowel that are not in stressed position. ... However, that the effect of position is realized differently in each of the major categories suggests that penultimate lengthening is not the correct generalization. When the vowel of investigation is long or precedes a prenasalized stop, V1 is significantly shorter in duration compared to V3, yet, there is no difference between V1 and V3 when the vowel of investigation is short. A penultimate lengthening analysis predicts that V3 would always be longer than V1, even for the lexically short vowels. Rather, these data suggest a general pattern of vowel reduction that does not produce short vowels less than around 50 ms in duration. However, the reduction analysis does not preclude the possibility that there is penultimate stress. It could simply be that the penultimate prominence results in shortening before the penultimate position. [p. 21] While penultimate stress certainly could be the cause of this durational difference, the alternative hypothesis should also be considered in future research.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Saamia (saam1283) is not in the catalog. Of the three works with stress in the title, two (Schwab & Dellwo 2017; Flege & Fletcher 1992) are Glottolog mis-assignments about Spanish stress perception and foreign accent, irrelevant; the third, Philippson 1991 (Tons et accent.., 542-pp Paris V thesis linked by Glottolog to 48 languages incl. Saamia), is print-only (theses.fr 'accessible: non', not on HAL) and its abstract describes the tone-to-penultimate-accent continuum of East African Bantu without placing Saamia. Beyond the title list, the language's Glottolog bibliography and the IULC Working Papers archive yielded open texts that were downloaded and read but are silent on word stress (Marlo 2019 Saamia NC phonology; Hieda 2016 AALL 10; Marlo 2008 Tura, which groups Saamia among predictable-tone Luyia dialects), plus the abstract of Marlo & Brown 2002 'Segmental duration in Lusaamia', which explicitly tests the Bantu penultimate-stress expectation acoustically but whose PDF is not attached (old IULC site gone; web.archive.org could not be reached by automated download). Print/search-only leads with the best chance of a stress statement: Botne, Ochwada & Marlo 2006 grammatical sketch (HathiTrust search-only; Harvard print), Chagas 1976 and Poletto 1998 (tonal studies). No the best new statement; no catalog change.fr, HAL, CiNii, TUFS, ScholarWorks IU and SAL.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Saamia is a tone language (verb tone predictable by mora position). The only study to address word stress is an instrumental duration study: it tested the general Bantu claim of penultimate stress and found that base (penultimate) long and pre-NC vowels are longer than the corresponding reduplicant vowels, but not short vowels, so the authors reject penultimate lengthening as the generalization while leaving open whether penultimate stress exists. Companion paper (Marlo 2002, fn. 24 p. 27): 'It remains unclear if stress plays a role in Lusaamia, which is a tone language.' If any word stress exists it would be penultimate, but no source asserts this for Saamia.
new_statements.exceptions: Durational asymmetry holds for long and pre-NC vowels but not for lexically short vowels (p. 16); final vowels show utterance-final lengthening (p. 16-17); polysyllabic shortening in reduplicated verbs (p. 17).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated infinitival verb forms (oxu-CVC-a and reduplicated oxu-CVCa-CVCa) read from a list by one speaker; utterance-final position, so word and utterance edges coincide. Tone system is the primary prosody; no noun data.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Lusaamia of the Kenyan side (Marlo's and Botne's consultant Hannington Ochwada, Funyula/Busia area; Marlo 2019 also Kenyan Saamia). Hieda 2016 is on Ugandan Saamia. The Ugandan variety Lugwe is sometimes grouped with it (Glottolog lists Saamya-Gwe as one dialect). No dialect split relevant to stress is reported.

new_statements.quote: [PDF p.413, ch.6 §2.1.6] Pour le groupe VII, vu la très grande diversité interne (plus d'une douzaine de dialectes sur un vaste territoire), il serait surprenant que tous les systèmes soient identiques. Mais nous ne pouvons à peu près rien en dire, si ce n'est que plusieurs ont un système prosodique du même type que le bukusu-masaaba, avec une mélodie BH (c'est au moins le cas du saamia et sans doute du logooli). [PDF p.78, Tableau II 'typologie prosodique'] "(a) : 5, (b) : 2" : shi (groupe I); rwanda/rundi, hangaza ?, shubi ?, ha ? (groupe II); saamia, bukusu (groupe VII).
new_statements.translation: [p.413] For group VII [Luhya], given the very great internal diversity (more than a dozen dialects over a vast territory), it would be surprising if all the systems were identical. But we can say almost nothing about them, except that several have a prosodic system of the same type as Bukusu-Masaaba, with a LH melody (this is at least the case of Saamia and probably of Logooli). [p.78, Table II 'prosodic typology', where (a) = number of distinct tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems and (b) = on disyllabic verbo-nominals] '(a): 5, (b): 2': Shi (group I); Rwanda/Rundi, Hangaza?, Shubi?, Ha? (group II); Saamia, Bukusu (group VII).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal (Saamia classed among languages with lexical tone patterns, Bukusu-type LH-melody system) and is SILENT on stress placement: it neither supports nor contradicts the hedged 'penultimate stress' remark of Marlo & Brown 2003 (existing statement, reading unclear or contradictory). the compilers inference from the theses.fr abstract ('silent on this language as far as can be seen; whether Saamia is in the sample cannot be determined') is now settled: Saamia IS in the sample (Tableau 1, p.71) but only as a poorly-known language mentioned on 4 pages, with no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson treats Saamia (E34, Luhya group VII) only in passing, from Chagas 1976: it is a language with lexical prosodic (tonal) distinctions — 5 distinct tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems, 2 on verbo-nominals — and a prosodic system 'of the same type as Bukusu-Masaaba with a LH melody' (his 'système accentuel à mélodie *BH', i.e. a restricted tone system in which a lexically marked mora takes a L-H melody). He says nothing about word stress, demarcative accent or the penultimate syllable in Saamia; the language has no analysis section and no annex entry (for Bukusu, the analysed relative of the same type, annex item 10 'status of the penultimate syllable' is 'néant' = none). The thesis's penultimate-accent discussion (ch.6 §3.5, abstract) concerns other languages (Swahili, Nyoro/Tooro, Sukuma etc.), not Saamia.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing (no stress statement for Saamia at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none; the author flags Saamia as poorly documented ('nous ne pouvons à peu près rien en dire') and Tableau II as not to be taken literally for imperfectly known languages (p.78)
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's 'saamia (E 34)' = Olusamia/Lusaamia of the Kenya-Uganda border (his only source is Chagas 1976 'The tonal structure of Olusamia', i.e. the Samia variety described in Hyman ed. 1976); treated as a poorly documented member of his group VII (Luhya) alongside Bukusu, Masaaba, Logooli, Nyore, Nyuli.

sources.quote: There is relatively little prior research on Saamia. The main works describing aspects of the structure of Saamia are Chagas (1976), Poletto (1998), Marlo (2002, 2004, 2006), Marlo & Brown (2002), Botne (2004), Botne et al. (2006), and Heida (2016).
sources.note: Segmental NC alternations only; 'Tone is not transcribed'; no occurrence of stress/penultimate/accent in text.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. & Aaron Brown. 2002. Segmental duration in Lusaamia: a phonetic study. IULC Working Papers Online 2(1) (ScholarWorks IU abstract record).
sources.quote: Besides segmental effects on other segments, this paper also touches on the effects of position and stress on vowel length within a given utterance. [...] Mean durations of pre-antepenultimate and penultimate position of the infinitival form of reduplicated CVC verbs are discussed. Since stress is claimed to be penultimate in many Bantu languages, one might expect penultimate vowels to be longer than vowels in other positions (Batibo 2000, Anyanwu 2001). This hypothesis is considered in light of the acoustic measurements.
sources.note: Abstract: 'Since stress is claimed to be penultimate in many Bantu languages, one might expect penultimate vowels to be longer than vowels in other positions..
